speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: EFFORT TO STOP HOSTILITIES BY EMBARGO ON SHIPMENT OF ARMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, according to the morning paper Great Britain is heading a number of nations in a proposal to put an embargo on the shipment of armaments to the disputants Bolivia and Paraguay. I understand that in this matter Great Britain seeks cooperation of the United States. I believe that we are not shipping any armaments, but that our people are very much interested in a movement of this kind. I have wondered whether the government could see its way clear to make a statement of endorsation or congratulation of Great Britain upon the stand she seems to be taking at this time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EFFORT TO STOP HOSTILITIES BY EMBARGO ON SHIPMENT OF ARMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was good enough to indicate to me that he purposed mentioning this matter on the orders of the day. While my personal view was that we might discuss the matter on the item I had left open in the estimates under the Department of External Affairs, namely the item concerning the League of Nations, I have prepared a short statement which I shall be very glad to make to the house at the moment, and further discussions may take place when that estimate is under consideration.

subtopic: EFFORT TO STOP HOSTILITIES BY EMBARGO ON SHIPMENT OF ARMS
speechtext: We passed that estimate when my right hon. friend was not in the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EFFORT TO STOP HOSTILITIES BY EMBARGO ON SHIPMENT OF ARMS
speechtext:
I thought the house desired to discuss the matter, and I left the item for that reason. If necessary I shall provide facilities for further discussion. The Associated Press dispatch which appeared in this morning's press indicates that Great Britain has taken steps to place an embargo on the shipment of arms to South American countries. I suppose the house recalls the position of members of the League of Nations with respect to matters of this kind. Article 23 of the covenant provides that the members of the League agree to entrust the league with the general supervision of the trade in arms and ammunition with the countries in which the control of this traffic is necessary in the common interest, subject to and in accordance with the provisions of international conventions existing or hereafter to be agreed upon. That, is the provision in the covenant of the League of Nations. It will be within the
memory of hon. members that last year we took action with respect to the International convention.
Canada signed the "International convention for the supervision of the international trade in arms and ammunition and in implements of war" at Geneva on June 17th, 1925, and, following approval by parliament, ratified the convention on May 8th, 1933, subject to the reservation that ratification shall not take effect until ratifications of the convention shall have been effective, in accordance with Article 41 of the convention, in respect of Austria, Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United States of America.
The object of the convention is to establish a general system of supervision and publicity for the international trade in arms and implements of war and to set up a special system for areas where special measures are gradually recognized to be necessary.
Some action has been taken. But as I shall presently indicate, for reasons that perhaps are well known no very effective action has been taken with respect to this matter among the nations of the world, primarily, I assume, because the convention is not yet in force, and will not become effective until four months after fourteen ratifications have been deposited by the signatory governments with the government of the French republic. So far the convention has been signed on behalf of thirty-seven countries and thirteen ratifications, including the Canadian ratification, have been received, but the majority of these are contingent upon ratification by the producing powers. Of the latter, the following have not yet ratified the convention-Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United States of America. His Majesty's governments in the United Kingdom and in Australia have made their ratifications contingent upon ratification by all producing countries. Our ratification was not dependent upon that qualification.
In February, 1933, His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom suggested to the league that action should be taken under the terms of article XI of the covenant to recommend that the various governments impose an embargo on the export of arms and ammunition to Bolivia and Paraguay. On that occasion the Canadian government notified its willingness to cooperate with other nations in concerting prohibition of export of armaments to Bolivia and Paraguay. A draft regulation to be signed by the governments in favour of this step was considered by the council and accepted by all the states members of the council, including the United Kingdom. A number of states made their acceptance

subject to acceptance of the declaration by a specified number of other states including the United States. The government of the latter country, however, were unable to impose an embargo until necessary legislation was passed by congress.
Yesterday, according to the press dispatches to which I referred, Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal of Great Britain, again brought the issue of an embargo on arms and ammunition to Bolivia and Paraguay before the council of the League of Nations, which is now in session at Geneva, expressing the hope that the council would adopt a resolution to consult the arms exporting countries as soon as possible. Press reports indicate that support for the United Kingdom government's proposal was promised by delegates from France, Italy, Spain, Argentina, Czechoslovakia and Australia, which is this year a member of the council as Canada was some years ago. The matter was postponed to a later session of the council "to be convoked as soon as possible." Press reports further indicate that a communication will probably be made to the following countries in addition to the great powers:	Canada, Australia,
Belgium, Chile, Denmark, Spain, Estonia, Greece, Latvia, Lithuania, Mexico, Holland, Persia, Poland, Rumania, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey and Yugoslavia. No official communication has yet been received by the Canadian government.
I certainly think, as the hon. member has said, that His Majesty's government in Great Britain is to be warmly congratulated and heartily commended for the action that has been taken. I assume that it is hardly necessary for me to add that in the event of the opportunity presenting itself Canada will participate favourably in any such action as may be taken in that regard.

On the orders of the day:

May I
inquire from the Minister of Agriculture if his department is in a position to give the house any information with regard to a serious outbreak of the disease known as glanders among horses in the province of Quebec, and particularly in the St. Johns district. Would the minister state how many animals have been destroyed, and if the situation is well in hand?

The hon. member for Cartier informed me that he was going to ask this question, and because of the uncertainty in the minds of many farmers I think it well to make a fairly detailed statement. There has been an outbreak of glanders in Quebec. The first traces of it appeared on November 1, 1933, in three horses imported by Guy C. Tillotson, Coaticook. Two gave suspicious reaction. They had been transported three hundred miles by truck to Coaticook.
On November 18, 1933, these horses were retested; two reacted and were slaughtered without compensation in accordance with the regulation.
On November 25, 1933, five horses from the same stable as the imported horses reacted and were slaughtered. On November 29 three horses also reacted on this owner's farm, so that the outbreak did not originate from the imported horses. Subsequently it has been found that this outbreak is almost certainly

Soldier Settlement Legislation
a carry-over from an outbreak dealt with three years ago in the Knowlton district, Quebec.
The disease is in a mild form. Very few clinical cases have been found and these so indefinite that suspicion was not aroused; hence glanders was not reported.
Reports of suspected glanders are received from time to time in different parts of Canada and in such cases all the owners' horses are tested with mallein. All imported horses are either accompanied by certificate or tested with mallein before entering Canada.
Immediate steps were taken to trace and test all contacts and as reactors were found this increased the work in tracing contacts from additional diseased horses.
One horse recently shipped from Alberta reacted in Quebec. When traced back its mate reacted. This case was traced back to an outbreak near Beiseker, Alberta, where opposition to giving information had been encountered which made difficult the tracing of all contacts.
This horse had not been in Quebec long and has no relation to the origin of the Quebec outbreak. All contacts in Alberta are being dealt with now.
The details as to compensation are as follows:
Compensation awarded in Ottawa records: 306 horses slaughtered, $23,316.
Compensation passed for payment, $16,980.61.
The latest information from Quebec, dated May 12, 1934, is as follows:
5,511 horses tested.
319 horses reacted.
224 infected premises.
$24,070.33 compensation awarded.
Since the outbreak developed, horses passing through the Montreal yards have been tested, the total number of horses tested being 1,783. The number of officers was gradually increased as the situation warranted. Experienced men were employed and, because of their experience, three were brought from the western provinces. The disease has been confirmed by post mortem examination and in laboratory small animals. The improvement shown during the last week to May 12 is indicated by the following figures: 476 horses tested; 3 reactors. That shows that the situation is well under control.

I regret that so much time is being taken to answer these questions. I first brought up this matter on March 26, when the house was in committee on the resolution. At that time I asked this question. which appears on page 1812 of Hansard:

As the government has not answered my question I suppose I am to understand that it does not intend to do any thing to improve home marketing conditions.
In fairness to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) I must say that he rose to answer my question but an hon. member on this side started to speak. subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The committee is discussing section 3, subsection (9), and I cannot see that this has anything to do with that subsection.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Subsection 9 reads:
The governor in council may from time to time authorize payment to the board, out of the consolidated revenue fund, of such sums of money as may be necessary for the purposes of this act.
The purpose^ of the act is stated in the title, which reads:
An act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith.
This is a bill to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and I am complaining about the decrease in home consumption and, therefore, in sales of natural products. I submit that what I am saying is perfectly relevant and in accord with subsection (9) of section 3. Under that subsection the governor in council may from time to time authorize payment to the board, out of the consolidated revenue fund, of such sums of money as may be necessary for the purposes of this act with regard to the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada. I submit that what I am now saying is quite relevant.
On May 8 I quoted some figures showing the decrease in the home consumption of apples, honey, eggs, dressed beef, concentrated milk, cheese, potatoes, peas, oats, barley, wheat and wheat flour. I gave figures showing the spread in prices in 1933 as compared with 1930, after which there was the following dialogue between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) and myself:
Mr. Pouliot: Just a moment; I am just concluding my remarks. I am sure the minister will answer.
Mr. Weir (Melfort) : My understanding was that with these statistics on record in Hansard an answer would be submitted to the hon. member for Temiscouata.
Mr. Pouliot: I thank you.

Marketing Act
That appears on page 2893 of Hansard of May 8. On the following day I asked a question of the minister which appears on page 2931 of Hansard and reads:
Mr. Pouliot: Is the minister ready to answer my question of yesterday?
Mr. Weir (Melfort): The principle under consideration in the wording of clause 9 is to confine the application of power to the creation of interprovincial and export trade.
The minister was answering another question. However, I do not blame him for that as there was a great rush of questions at that time. I thought I was very reasonable when I waited several more days. On page 3094 of Hansard of May 16, the following appears:
Mr. Pouliot: I should like to ask the minister if he can give me some explanation with regard to the decrease in the consumption of apples, honey, eggs, fresh beef, concentrated milk, cheese, potatoes, wheat, oats, barley and wheat flour, as compared with the previous year. I take the liberty of asking this question because on May 8 the minister said that an answer would be given me in this connection.
Mr. Weir (Melfort) : The officials of the department have been working since May 8 to gather the information requested by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I have inquired as to the matter on a number of occasions, the last time this morning, but the work is not yet completed. We hope to have the information in the very near future. There has been a very great deal of work in this connection.
Mr. Pouliot: Would the minister be kind enough to tell me if it will be completed before the bill is reported by the committee?
Mr. Weir (Melfort): I believe it will be completed this week.
That was the day before yesterday. In the Hansard of yesterday, at page 3121, the following appears:
Mr. Pouliot: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture if he now has available the information that I have been seeking from him for some time? Yesterday he was kind enough to give me a ray of hope when he said that he hoped to have the information in the very near future. What I want is information with regard to the decrease in the home consumption of several farm products which have been mentioned several times in Hansard. I hope the minister will be kind enough to tell me, first, if w-e still have a local market for these commodities; secondly, the reason for the decrease in the home consumption of such products; and thirdly, the remedy, if any, which has been applied by the government to prevent that decrease which has been taking place since 1930.
Mr. Weir (Melfort): I regret that the information asked for has not yet been completed. I am sure the hon. member will realize when the answer is brought down that there was perhaps more -work entailed in getting the information than he had in mind when he asked for it, but I hope it will be in shape to be brought down at the beginning of next week, if not to-morrow.
Mr. Pouliot: I thank the hon. gentleman, and if I can be of any assistance to the officers of his department in cooperating with them I shall be very glad to do so.
I would suggest to the staff of the Minister of Agriculture that they should cooperate with the staff of the bureau of statistics. They would get the same information which I have received and which is official. The information in regard to home consumption was given to me by the bureau of statistics, and for the two items I found the price in the Year Book, while for the other items I have divided the value of exports by the quantity in order to arrive at an average price. The quantity of decrease has been multiplied by that average price for 1930 and 1933 respectively. It is very simple to work it out. If the members of the minister's staff are not strong enough on mathematics they might consult the treasury board or the mathematicians in the architects branch of the Department of Public Works, who- I am sure would make the calculation for them. It is a matter of applying the simple rules of arithmetic, and it ought to be easy for them to ascertain whether the figures are correct or not. I assure the committee that it is a matter of utmost importance, because what has been discussed until now is only the external trade. The only figures in regard to internal trade are those that are to be found on March 26 and May 8, and in respect of May 8 I have been more than generous, because I have subtracted the amount of exports of butter and pork meat from the amount of decrease in home consumption of same. If the exports of butter and pork products were added to the decrease in home consumption, we should have a real idea of the decrease or the price spread as between 1933 and 1930 in connection with those two products.
I am not going to dwell very long on this matter, but this is my contention. I maintain that it is because of the loss in external trade that we have a loss in internal trade, and the loss in external trade is something fearful. Our external trade is only one-third of what it was in 1930. It may be said that it is just as true for imports as for exports. The point is that it has created a great deal of unemployment, and here we come again to the high tariff walls which have been erected around this country, which have been an obstacle to external trade, and which explain the decrease in our home trade.
Mark you, sir, the decrease in exports from Canada from 1930 until the present time amounts to over a billion and a half dollars.
Marketing Act

How much unemployment has that meant throughout Canada? The reason there is a decrease in consumption in Canada, although the hon. gentleman presiding over the Department of Agriculture may not be willing to admit it, is that the people have no purchasing power; they have not enough money to buy apples, honey, grain, vegetables, cheese and other farm products. And it is because of the loss of purchasing power among the people that the farmers are suffering, notwithstanding that the population is larger than it was in 1930. If the population were smaller, and if the prices of farm products were higher, I would not insist on this point; I would say that the people were not buying luxuries. But these twelve articles which are mentioned there are primary farm products. The sales should be at least as much as they were in 1930. There is no excuse for the decrease, because many of these products cost less now than they did before.
From my point of view therefore it is of the utmost importance, in order that I may understand the working of the bill, to have answers to the following three questions. Have we still got our local trade in these commodities? The Prime Minister stated last year, and he repeated it time and time again, that we still have our local trade, our local market. But if the home consumption of these farm products has decreased to such an extent, can it be said that we still have our local market, as the Prime Minister stated categorically and emphatically a year ago? That is the first question.
The second question is this: What have been the causes of that decrease in home consumption? There must be a reason for it. Was I wrong in stating that the decrease in external trade, due to the high tariff policy of the government, has been responsible for a decrease in internal trade, which depends to some extent upon the purchasing power of people working in the manufacturing industries, who must have the money necessary to buy these farm products.
In the third place, if the reason is not as I suggest, what is it, and what remedies have been taken by this government to prevent that decrease in home consumption? I ask this question because up to now the discussion has been about external trade only, and I should like this government to give us an explanation so that we may see whether as a matter of fact such a relationship exists between external and internal trade.
Trade matters are very difficult. It is like clockwork. You can remove one wheel from a clock and it might rvork just the same, but it would be either faster or slower and would
IMr. Pouliot.]
not keep time. But if you remove all the wheels from the clock how can it work? I do not want to say anything unpleasant to the minister, but I tell him here and now that I have been most patient, for these figures have been on Hansard for over a month and a half. I am entitled to an answer after all the care I have taken preparing the figures. It could be done much more expeditiously by the officers of the minister's department, and I say that if they have not these figures at hand they deserve only one thing, and that is to be put out at once. They should prepare the right information for the minister, and there is no excuse for their not doing so. They must inform the minister accurately and if they fail to do so then they are not fit for the job and should be put on direct relief. But I believe that they can do that work provided the minister will tell them seriously, "I want that information at once. It is my duty as a minister of the crown to supply every member of this house with that information, and I am telling you to bring it to me at once, because your job is at stake." If the minister would take that attitude he would find at once that the answer was, "Ready, aye, ready; we are ready."
I hope that as I have been so lenient and patient, having waited a month and a half for that information-I have not insisted before ; I have merely reminded the minister that I wanted the information for my electors -he will now take proper steps to have it prepared and submitted before six o'clock to-day.

No free man shall be seized, or imprisoned, or dispossessed, or outlawed, or in any way brought to ruin: we will not go against any man, nor send against him save by legal judgment of his peers, or by the law of the land. ... To no man will we sell, or deny, or delay right or justice.

I am following the remarks
made by the minister under this section in connection with prohibition. The fruit and honey act forbids the marketing of inferior grades but this section forbids the marketing of any grade, it is a total prohibition. Sometimes a homely illustration is even 'better than a reference to constitutional procedure. I have in mind a couple of men who go out and rent a field of ten acres from a farmer. They put in potatoes and spend the whole season cultivating their crop. In the fall when they want to sell they have to take the market price because they have no facilities for storing. They take their money, pay their rent and the remainder is their compensation for their labour. These men might be prohibited from selling their potatoes or the sale might be postponed for six months. Potatoes are not like wheat which can be carried over. Potatoes grown in certain soils must be sold1 quite early in the season. I ask the minister what those men are to do when they find themselves forbidden to sell the produce they have grown. This illustrates the great difference between this bill and the British act which was supposed to give us a precedent for our legislation. The British act is fundamentally based upon the encouragement of production. Mr. Elliot's ideal is to get them to produce more. If a man produces more-than the market will stand, Mr. Elliot does: not tell him that he cannot sell, he tells the-man in Canada or the man in Denmark that he cannot ship so much. From the very nature of things, this matter is important because we are an exporting country. I should like to know from the minister what is to happen in the case of a man who has produced a perishable article and is told that he cannot sell it?

The point that

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Charlotte pointed out the conditions which existed in his constituency, and he is quite correct. Let me point out to the minister how this thing might work out. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) stated that one province had already appointed a provincial board. He did not name that province but I shall give it now-it is the province of New Brunswick. A board has been appointed there and I claim it has been sitting without authority. How is that board constituted? The natural producer is represented by a commission merchant. I am not going to say that he is not a farmer and does not know what he is doing, but the fact is that he is a commission merchant. The chairman is the deputy minister of agriculture of the province and the third member is a sardine canner. The original producers are not represented at all. I have every faith in the honesty of the members of this board, but I do oppose the principle of appointing as a member of a provincial board an exporter and purchaser of the natural products. How is such a person going to distinguish between his own interests and those of the natural producer from whom he purchases the natural products to be canned for export? This shows how this thing can be abused. I do not say this will happen with this department, but it may happen with the departments of certain governments. I believe these three men are absolutely honest but I am opposed to the principle of appointing men who are themselves interested in the export of an article while the original producer is not represented at all. Now that act passed by New Brunswick is being put into operation before the federal act is passed giving them authority to act, and they are acting in both

Marketing Act
respects, export and interprovincial trade. I am merely pointing this out to show the minister what abuses can creep in under this act.

speechtext: As I said before, if we fixed any percentage of votes or of production it might be taken by the provincial authorities that we were going out of our way to tell them what they should do. My own opinion was that any reasonable body of men would make certain, when such drastic steps were to be taken, that there would be a percentage of producers and also of production.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I understood the minister to say that 75 per cent was provided for; now it appears that it is only possible. If they choose
to ask for 75 per cent they may or may not get it, but they do not have to. There is the difference between this and the British act, which looks after the interests of the minority.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Their problem is very different from ours. They have one government instead of ten, and it was to get over that difficulty that we dropped any set percentage, trusting that any provincial government would have as good judgment as the federal.

speechtext: I understand that. But I suggested, when I was speaking a day or two ago, that that might have been got around by the dominion government putting forward some sort of skeleton scheme to which every province would have to subscribe in the main lines if they wished the cooperation of the dominion. Without interfering with provincial jurisdiction, the minister could simply say that if the province wanted dominion cooperation they must agree to such and so. The federal government did that in connection with old age pensions. They did not enforce any obligation on the province but simply said, "If you do so and so, here is our skeleton scheme and we will do so and so"; and every province, without a great deal of trouble, saw their way to agree to the scheme. The provision made under the British act might be put into this scheme. Under the British system it has to be two-thirds of the people voting at the poll; there must not be less than 50 per cent of a vote of all producers; and there must be at least two-thirds in quantity produced. I would ask the minister whether he could not qualify the words "and the agency through which." The idea is to allow probably the milk and fruit people of British Columbia, let us say, to deal through their associations.

speechtext: That was not the intent.

Through some cooperative agency. The language is much too broad. If you say through any agency, it leaves it open to some tinpot commission agent to get the whole agency for some product in his province, and it is these things that arouse suspicions in the minds of people. The dominion board may prescribe "any" agency through which the product must be marketed. Think what that might involve. It might involve the decision that it should be done through the local board; but the board has
Marketing Act

power to delegate it to someone else. It might involve its being done through a cooperative association or a farmers' institute, or it might involve a man with political pull who has a petty agency, and it would amount then to giving him a rakeoff. I think we have for the past three months followed pretty much the line the hon. gentleman has suggested. We started out by trying to make the bill specific enough to include all conditions, but we were forced, because of representations made and the great difference in the conditions we had to meet, to do just as he has said, namely, to set up a skeleton bill which would make it possible for cooperation between provinces and the dominion, so that one could provide for domestic marketing and the other interprovincial or export trade.
I agree with the hon. member that if we had one government instead of ten that could be very easily overcome; but I think we have a perfect safeguard in the fact that the local board has to be set up by the producers themselves, and I suggest that no one would have their interests more at heart than the producers themselves. The purpose of putting in the agency was not at all to make it easy for all the products to go through a certain cooperative agency; I do not think the great body of producers themselves would advocate that. Perhaps the picture that illustrates it best is this. One farmer may be quite a large producer with a large volume of product to market. If he has a considerable volume to market he can make a better bargain with different channels of trade, because if they get a greater volume it will be less costly for them to market the product when they know the quality.
We are really making it possible, if the growers wish to organize so that they may have a greater volume, that they can have the advantage in the different channels of trade.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Would not the words "time and place" cover that?

(Mr. Neill.]
than the Victoria market. It was just to clear up that point that the word "agency" was inserted.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The minister is making it pretty clear that the bill as presented is the result of representations largely from special groups, groups that come from particular localities.

So that nothing that is not quite accurate may be put on record, what I intended to say was this: We made use of all known information after a careful study of the different acts in force. We felt that it would be to the advantage of the primary producers to have a marketing bill under which we could set up a marketing board. A great deal of information was then before us as to the problems with which we had to deal and in the preparation of this bill we have been in touch with private individuals, the trade and cooperative organizations, in order to add to the information that was already ours. That was the way in which the representations were made. This bill, it has been stated, I believe, by hon. members on both sides, is the result of demands made upon me as Minister of Agriculture in Regina when the cooperatives met there last summer.
I am quite certain, however that the cooperatives themselves would be the last to make such a suggestion because I stated there I felt we should have competition in trade but on the fundamental principles we disagreed. After the frank discussions we had, a committee met with me in the Royal York hotel at the time of the Royal Winter fair and there again I emphasized that point very clearly, but the preparation of this bill was proceeding much earlier than the meeting that was held at Regina. We were working on a definite plan to assist in the marketing of the products of all primary producers; we gathered all the information possible from cooperative organizations and others and of course we always welcomed any suggestions whether they came from cooperatives or not. But this bill was not prepared simply to meet the wishes of cooperative or special organizations.

speechtext:
I think the
illustrations that have been given in the course of the discussion make clear what I am saying. measure to be in force to-morrow? The applications under it would come to the minister presumably largely from interested groups in western Canada.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I would say not.
As a matter of fact I have more requests from eastern Canada.

speechtext:
Perhaps I
might be permitted to continue what I had in mind to say, because the impression I am getting very strongly as a result of communications that are coming in to me is that while western producers feel that they may be able to assist themselves by presenting a number of schemes which will be approved by the minister, those schemes all have the effect of limiting production; that unquestionably is one of their effects.

speechtext:
That is one point
on which my hon. friend and I evidently seem still to disagree. I do not see how this bill would in any way limit production. It is simply to regulate the marketing of the product.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
It is only a
step from restricting or prohibiting the sale of commodities to limiting production. That is the inevitable effect and it is simply playing upon words to say that regulation will not restrict production because any regulation that will restrict the sale or offering for sale or prohibit the offering for sale of commodities will certainly very shortly affect and limit production. Let us assume that some organizations in the west have their plans approved, and that they are satisfied with them but that producers in other parts of Canada have not made similar applications for similar schemes, have not similar schemes, and are free to continue to sell their commodities as they please. What will the effect of that be? I am being told by one person after another that they believe the effect of this measure will be to sacrifice the production of the west to the profits of the east; that is the impression which is becoming more and more general as to the result of this legislation. In its actual working out it will mean that the production of the west will be sacrificed to the profits of the east.
I put it in that clear way so that this possibility may come clearly before the committee.
I say that the possibility is there with regard to commodities regulated in any part of Canada and not equally regulated in other parts, that the production of regulated commodities may be sacrificed to commodities that are not regulated in other localities. That only brings out the wisdom of any
regulations, if they are to be effective, being made by parliament, not by local groups, so that the regulations will cover Canada from one end of the country to the other. If they do not they are bound to have the effect that the production of those having to do with regulated products will be sacrificed to the profits of those who produce commodities that are not regulated.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The right hon.
gentleman is surely not serious in his statement. If we consider the picture that he has in mind, it means that the western producers themselves will so act that they will restrict the production and the marketing of their goods to help the east. That is what the right hon. gentleman said.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Might I give a concrete illustration? Supposing you have a group of producers in one part of British Columbia: in order to work out a scheme that will bring everyone into an organization-

speechtext: In British Columbia.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: -in one locality in British Columbia, in whatever portion of the province it may be, and assume that they get the minister to approve their scheme and he approves it, but in Nova Scotia there is no similar scheme and the producers there go on producing and selling just as they have been doing in the past. subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Would the producers in British Columbia not be credited with having sufficient intelligence to look after their own interests in any scheme they might submit?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I think what will happen under this legislation is that only a local point of view will be taken of anything done under it. The national view may fail to present itself at all.

speechtext:
We are suffering
under heavy difficulties in trying to get this agricultural bill through. First, it is before the worst committee on top of earth one could find-the committee of the whole House of Commons; that is difficulty number one. I do not think anybody can put this bill through as it stands or explain it properly. If I did not know a little about it I would be rather up the flue as regards understanding it with
Marketing Act

all these amendments and subamendments as it stands now. We have one crop of printed amendments brought down by the minister, another typed crop submitted to the chair, and there you are. speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
Who is guffawing
' now? My hon. friend knows that what I say is true.

speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman is really serious.

speechtext:
Serious! The very
first criticism I had of this bill was that the government had grabbed off too much; too many fingers in the pie, too many cooks spoiling the broth. The minister has told us he has been all over Canada getting advice. That is all right, but in trying to please everyone he pleases no one. You know the old story about the fellow that lost his ass in the bargain. I say that the ministry is putting the Minister of Agriculture in a position that I have been in several times myself. I venture the guess that the Minister of Agriculture, as long as he occupies the position he now does, will never be caught again with this kind of agricultural bill going direct to the committee of the whole house. Now, might I suggest that if the minister has any estimates or anything like that to put through, he in the meantime have this bill consolidated 'by the Justice department; then let us start in Monday morning with a bill that we can understand. Another difficulty was embodying so many natural products in an agricultural bill as forecast in the throne speech-fish, flagpoles, saw logs, etc. At the beginning it was proposed to in-

elude minerals also. Why do they not include hydro power also? Whisky is in, and beer.

speechtext: First let me tell the minister there has been no concerted effort to block the bill, and as far as misinterpreting the bill is concerned, not even the ministry have been able to interpret what they mean by the bill. Does this government think for one moment that simply because they bring down a bill and because there are 138 hon. members sitting behind the Prime Minister, we of necessity must swallow the bill and may not offer just criticisms of it? Any criticisms I have offered I think have been quite just, and time has not permitted me yet to say all I want to say against it. The very fact that to a bill of some twenty-one sections we have eighteen amendments shows the situation. And we are not through with it yet, we are still dealing with subsection (a) of section 4. I resent the attitude of the minister in saying that anyone is attempting to block this bill. The British system exempts from the scheme the small, petty producers whose enumerations, and everything else, would be a perfect curse to the department, and of no earthly use at all. They leave him out of the picture altogether, but having once passed the scheme everybody is subject to any order, as they properly should be. We do the reverse. We put under the act everybody who owns a cow, three or four chickens or a pig, and he is subject to all the regulations and forms. It would take an army to enumerate them. Then, we realize the absurdity of the thing, and under this section we take the power to exempt these people, or anyone, from any determination or order; but it means giving them each an exemption under each and every order. I object to that procedure. This is the British system as indicated in paragraph (b) subsection 1, section 6 of the Agricultural Marketing Act of Great Britain:
Every scheme shall provide for the following matters, that is to say:-
(b) for exempting from all or any of the provisions of the scheme producers and sales of such classes or descriptions . . .
And so on. I believe there have been only two or three schemes formulated, one of which is a dairy scheme. They exempt anyone having less than four cows. Then, under the poultry scheme they exempt anyone selling less than twenty-five eggs at a time. Exempt those people, and you save an infinity of trouble; you save a lot of. people a lot of trouble, and you play the game fairly. A basic principle is not at stake, at all. This merely calls for a little common sense in carrying out the provision, and the prevention of any imputation of unfairness.

Under the pooling system there was, of course, an understanding that when the crop was sold the proceeds would be divided equally, having regard to grade, varying freight rates, and so

But it should be made very clear to them that this is an entirely different scheme, and that it does not provide for dividing up equally the proceeds of the crop. I just wonder how far either the local board or the dominion board is prepared to go in the way of compensation. Are they prepared, as was asked by my hon. friend from South Battleford (Mr. Vallance), to bear the storage charges, for instance, of farmers who are compelled by an order of the board to withhold their grain from the market? A very common method of taking our wheat to the elevator is by truck, by hired truck, it may be, and have it delivered immediately to the local elevator. Under the regulations issued by the local board a farmer may not be able to deliver his wheat to the local elevator. Are we prepared to assume the cost of storage involved and all the extra costs of handling and so forth, to which the farmer will be put in case he is not allowed to put his wheat on the market at a given time? speechtext: Might I ask the Prime Minister a question, which comes up n different places in the consideration of this oil'l? Does the Prime Minister say that the federal government has .power to give to any province a power which it does not already possess under the British North America Act?

No, that is exactly what I did not say. I tried to make it perfectly clear. Section 91 deals with peace, order and good government and then states:
. . . and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section-
The federal parliament is given exclusive legislative authority over the twenty-nine subjects which follow. Then, with respect to section 92, it says that the provinces shall have exclusive power over the matters therein mentioned. What the right hon. gentleman I trust did not understand was that I was suggesting for a moment that action taken by the parliament of Canada could confer upon the provinces legislative jurisdiction which under section 92 they do not possess, or that any action taken by a province in the exercise of its exclusive powers could confer a power upon the dominion.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Absolutely. And there is no reason why the instrument for the purpose of effecting the will of the federal parliament might not, with consent, be a province or anyone else, or that the agent to effect the will of a province might not be the federal power or anyone it might select. That is the whole suggestion. The bill is based upon that appreciation of it. But I should like to make it perfectly clear to the hon. gentleman that I would agree with him, and I trust he does not think I am suggesting that there would be any power in this parliament to give larger powers to the provinces than the constitution affords, or that there can be a diminution of provincial powers by acts of this parliament. The statute of Westminster provides that this parliament has not power

Marketing Act
to lessen or abridge or expand the legislative powers conferred by the British North America Act upon the provincial legislatures on the one hand and the federal parliament on the other.

speechtext:
May I then
ask this concrete question? The second of the exclusive powers given to the dominion is the regulation of trade and commerce. Would the Prime Minister say that the dominion could in any way confer upon any body within a province or upon the province itself the power to regulate trade and commerce in any particular or to any extent?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: In the case of Parsons vs. Citizens' Insurance Company the privy council held that the words "trade and commerce" in the statute, paragraph 2 of section 92, are to be construed as they have been previously construed as used in a statute passed in the reign of Queen Anne. Later, in the insurance reference following that decision, which held that statutory conditions in fire insurance policies were within the power of the provincial legislatures, the privy council held that our insurance acts were ultra vires and that the words "trade and commerce," while including insurance, did not mean any one branch of trade. That was the limitation placed upon them in the two cases. I do not suggest that the words "trade and commerce" mean that the parliament of Canada could by any legislative act confer upon the legislature of any province the power to enact legislation with respect to trade and commerce as the meaning of those words has been interpreted by the privy council. But I do say that the dominion parliament in the exercise of its jurisdiction with respect to trade and commerce can confer upon any instrument that it selects the necessary power to act as its agent in the carrying out of its legislative power under trade and commerce.

for coal mined on Vancouver island. There is a press record of there being a meeting with the minister of the eastern British Columbia coal people, the Alberta coal people and I think some of the eastern men who are suggesting increased subventions for themselves.
I have no objection to that; that is their problem. I see it is stated in the press that so far as Nova Scotia is concerned things are shaping well for a boom year in the Cape Breton coal industry, according to the Hon. Michael Dwyer, Minister of Public Works and Mines for the province.
I will just comment in passing that the coal output of Vancouver island is going down once more. The last record I have of it is for February, when there was a decrease of 21 per cent from the same month last year. That is an increasing trouble.
The cost to the government of assistance to Nova Scotia coal mines increased from $228,000 in 1931 to $1,447,000 in 1933, and in the case of Alberta and the Crowsnest pass from $212,000 to $228,000; for Saskatchewan the cost exactly doubled. These are all substantial increases. But the amount for subsidy for bunker and export coal for Vancouver island decreased in the same period from $36,756 to $26,952. There was a bonus of one dollar per ton on export coal, but there was no movement of export coal in 1933 and practically none in 1932. It was anticipated that this bonus of one dollar per ton for export coal would produce a trade of approximately 50,000 tons. I think the Prime Minister will recall that being said to him by a delegation that waited on him, but unfortunately, owing to perhaps unforeseen and unpreventable matters, the depression and war in- the South American republics, that trade has not eventuated. The trade in fact has totally disappeared. I suggest that in the case of Vancouver coal the subsidies have not been successful, or not successful at all events to the same extent as in the east, and I would suggest that the bunker coal subsidy should be raised from fifty cents to one dollar a ton. That is not very high considering that coal carried on the railways gets as high as two dollars a ton, and that the subsidy is paid on the long ton in the case of Vancouver island and on the short ton in the case of Nova Scotia coal. I know, because I have been in communication with him, that the minister has been kind enough to consider this matter, and I would just like a short statement from him or an assurance that the matter is still not finally settled, and I should like to know what hopes he has of being able to meet our views in this case.

The amount would not be very great. It would even then fall very far short by something like one-third of the amount estimated to be given in the beginning.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The subvention given to
Vancouver island coal at the present time is, as has been stated by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), fifty cents on bunker coal and one dollar per ton on coal for export. When these subventions were arranged after conferences with members on both sides of the house representing the locality and with the owners of the coal mines and some representatives of labour it was deemed at that time that the assistance then granted would be of a very substantial character. The operators depended in large measure upon the coal they would be able to export from the island into South American countries. However, experience has shown that that trade did not materialize. I doubt if any coal has been exported because, for reasons that are well known to members of this committee, the assistance to that movement could not apply to the United States.
Then difficulties also arose by reason of the ships from the orient, particularly from Japan, double bunkering. That resulted in a contraction of the market for coals from the island. At the present time, by reason of the changed conditions in the coal trade, largely brought about by the operation of the laws that have come into force in the United States, it has been found desirable and' necessary to give further study to these subventions, having regard to the increased price of United States coals under the N.R.A. That matter is still under review, and it is my hope that assistance this year to the coal mining industry of Canada will be maintained at least to the same extent as last year, but at a very much reduced cost to the treasury. It is obvious, of course, that by reason of the increased price of United States coal our mines will not and need not expect the same amount of assistance they received in the years past.

I have before me a child

Protested to the Hon. R. B. While appreciating the good work the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare was doing in the child and family welfare field', it protested its action in acquiescing in the Dominion government closing its division on child welfare. Tile Calgary Council on Child and Family Welfare felt that instead of attempting to assume the duties of the state the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare should have been a factor in striving to develop and strengthen the work of the government along the lines so ably begun and developed by Doctor Helen MacMurchy, while chief of the Child Welfare division.
In 1926 a protest came in from the different medical councils and from the county associations because the death rate among the children in Canada was so high, and maternal mortality was also very great. Many complaints were received. Doctor MacMurchy took the matter up in 1926 when the greatest number of complaints came in, and by her efforts the rate of child mortality, which was ten per cent that year, was greatly reduced. In the last three or four years the maternal mortality has also been considerably reduced. I do not say that this is due to the activities of Doctor MacMurchy's department, but I think the work is being amply provided for by the provincial government. I do not think the work should be taken out of the hands of the Department of Health; surely, if this is a medical department, a doctor and not some person who is merely a graduate of Queen's university should be in charge of the situation. While such graduates may be extremely capable, as I believe they are, and very enthusiastic over the work-and I have no fault to find in that regard-when we come to make an investigation from a medical standpoint, surely that requires a doctor and not some graduate of Queen's university with the degree of B.A. or M.A.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The matter to which the hon. member has referred is one of very great importance not only to this chamber but to every citizen of Canada. Doctor Helen MacMurchy was head of a division, if it might be called by that name. She retired, having reached the compulsory retiring age. The question that the minister had to consider with the aid of the deputy and his assistant was whether it was desirable to link the activities of the department with that of the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare which had been doing the direct service. It will be remembered that the dominion does no part of the direct service, the provinces are concerned with that. And it is under the direction of the provincial boards of health that the work in detail is carried on. The federal department has no doctors that go

into the homes, no medical attendants that visit the communities; but the provinces maintain their health centres and provide medical attention in municipalities and communities. The child welfare council is sustained by private subscriptions, largely from insurance companies because they are interested in the prolongation of human life and in the general welfare of the state. On the advice of the deputy minister, and having gone into the matter with care, the minister submitted that the best interests of the country would be served by at lea^t making the experiment. It must be recalled that the major part of this money in the child welfare division was paid as salaries. The resolution to wThich the hon. gentleman directed attention was received by me. It does not represent, I am sorry to say, very exact knowledge with respect to the matter. Had they taken the trouble to make inquiry they would not have passed the resolution in the terms in which it was passed. The fact is that the appropriation by this house for the child welfare division was largely utilized for salaries-that is, the federal side- while the provinces were carrying on the work they were, and the child welfare council the detail work to which I have referred. This is an experiment, if you may designate any agreement of this type as such, to coordinate the efforts of the state, in a matter which is largely within the jurisdiction of the provinces, with private effort. It has been exceedingly successful and I believe will result in great benefit, much greater than could result from maintaining the word "division" for the purpose of paying a salary to an official who might be at the head of it.

I am not
objecting to the increase in the grant, because I am not at all familiar with the change that has taken place, but I know it is the only grant to organizations of this kind that has been increased. I am not aware of the additional work that is being thrown upon the officers in charge of this organization. I have sometimes wondered if it would not be well to leave these services to the provinces. But heretofore we have been making these grants.
I want to refer to No. 242, mental hygiene. There has been a paring down of this grant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The ten per cent reduction, that is all.

Not only
this year but in former years. It seems to me rather strange that the appropriation for so important a work as that of mental hygiene, with which many of us are quite familiar,

Supply-Miscellaneous-Child Welfare
should be reduced. The propaganda they have carried on is of great benefit. I do not see why that should not be done by the provinces, but we have established the principle of assisting these organizations. I do not understand why one in particular is chosen, child welfare, which is certainly a provincial undertaking, to receive an increased grant, while the others are cut the usual ten per cent that runs through all the appropriations this year. I can hardly agree with the statement made by the Prime Minister that this is of sufficient importance to warrant an increase at this particular time, if the others are to be cut down. If the others are to be treated in the same way, I have no objection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If I do not interrupt, it
is a lesser sum of money that is being used; this contribution, which was used in the welfare division for one purpose, namely for salaries, is now being used for the purpose of promoting the work, without any additional staff. The minister is not here this evening. I have not brought with me the correspondence, because I had not expected to be dealing with it. If the committee desires I am content that it stand in order that they may have the information.

I am not claiming that this
grant should not be given, but I feel that looking after medical health is the duty of the provinces. The rate of maternal mortality in Canada is extremely high, 5-8 per thousand. In Italy it is only 2-7. We are an extremely barbarous country in regard to maternal mortality. In infant mortality the rate for Australia is 47 per 1,000 and for Canada, 89, almost twice as much. New Zealand is 35 per 1,000. I do not say this grant should not be given, but I do say it should be given to some medical department or some doctor who would have charge. The Prime Minister says they do not come in contact with the individual; that is true, but I have some seventy-five different books and publications of different types-not all with me-that are sent out through the provinces, especially Ontario; I cannot speak for the other provinces. These are paid for by this organization. It is said they are free, and I think that is right. The grant from this government is, I believe $3,600, while the insurance companies give about $10,000, and churches and other organizations, such as the. Rotary club, also contribute until they have altogether about $30,000. This organization is operating as a federal government organization for medical health. I cannot understand how any person who was formerly a stenographer, I do not care if she is
a graduate of Queen's, can take charge of a medical department. This is medical literature; it ought to be written by doctors. There are plenty of doctors in Toronto or Ottawa who are on relief, and this work should be done by medical men. I would have no objection, for that matter, if the grant were cut off entirely, because I think Hon. Mr. Robb was quite capable of looking after Ontario without any assistance from any graduate of Queen's.

I am at a loss to think
what better deserves our consideration than the matter which I understand we are now dealing with. In my home town of New Glasgow we have had for some years a baby clinic. That institution is visited daily by the doctors, and once or twice a week children, from a week old to three years or thereabouts, are brought there by parents or nurses and weighed and measured and records kept of their growth. The doctor gives the mother advice as to food, care and treatment. In my judgment that is a most important and valuable service, yet we talk about a few thousand dollars for it and we throw away $300,000 annually on the League of Nations without fifteen cents' worth of return to this country. I put these two expenditures before you as a matter of contrast; which better deserves the support of this house and this government and this country? Any man who gives the matter consideration must reach but one conclusion.
None of this money goes to the institution the hon. member speaks of-not a nickel.

Well, we are aiding the
provincial government. This is a vote in aid, as I understand it.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not this one.

The whole objection
we have to this is the duplication of service between the dominion and the provinces. We agree that it is a very important work, but as far as the work of this department is concerned in western Canada we know nothing about it. We hear about our own provincial work, and the work carried on in the provinces, but we do not hear about the work carried on by the dominion. It may be done down here in the east, but we do not know. Who pays the salaries, who are getting the salaries, and how much is paid in salaries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is aware that the Department of Health came
3204	COMMONS
Supply-Miseellaneous-Child Welfare
into being during the term of the Union government, and the child welfare division was established. In 1928 the Department of Health was allied with the Department of Pensions. The functions of the Department of Health, federally, certainly to some extent overlap the functions and duties discharged by the provincial boards of health. But the federal body was to be a coordinating body, and ever since it came into being it has brought to this city once a year the heads of the health departments of the provinces. Here, under the direction of the deputy minister, they have met together, discussed their problems, decided upon uniformity of regulations and legislation, and, if the hon. member, who is a medical man, would take the trouble to look into the matter, he would find that the services they have rendered to this country are incalculable. It has brought about uniformity of action; it has brought about improvement in what I may term sanitation, and in public health standards. It has resulted in the formulation of uniform policies.
The hon. member who spoke about the literature distributed in Ontario, the dental clinics which operate the provinces, and the efforts made to supply prenatal care in communities far removed from the larger centres, is fully aware of the fact that the federal administration has been responsible for bringing together the representatives of the health departments of all the provinces, and formulating the very policies to which he has referred, to the end that a measure of uniformity and the best known practice with respect to these matters should prevail. The hon. member for Willow Bunch is quite correct in saying that naturally in the western provinces they come more closely in contact with the provincial authorities, but the cooperative effort that is made on the part of the federal and provincial authorities to arrive at uniform standards and to improve working conditions with respect to the development of health policies any medical officer in any of the western provinces will tell you has been exceedingly great. I know that from my own observations when I was actively associated with the work of the Red Cross at a time when they were establishing hospitals in the very remote sections of northern Alberta and British Columbia. One knows, for instance, of the work of the voluntary organization which has been meeting in this city, the Victorian Order of Nurses, founded by Lady Aberdeen. Of course, they do work for one of the insurance companies for which they are paid, but in addition to that, so far as they can, they look after the 
various sections of the country. And the coordinating effort of the federal Department of Health has ensured the prevention of duplication of effort on the part of voluntary organizations with governmental instrumentalities. That has been great in the northern part of the western provinces. I can only assure the committee that if further knowledge is desired as to the details of the working out of this matter, the minister, who did not know this subject would be discussed to-night, would be glad to supply it. But with respect to salaries the point is that instead of appointing a successor to the late head and maintaining salaries it was decided to use that money for the purpose of actual work with the children, as the present child welfare council has been doing.
I deprecate the statement of the hon. member for North Wellington (Mr. Blair), with respect to the graduate from Queen's having once been a stenographer, and I think upon reconsideration he will withdraw it. Lord Russell of Killowen, one of the most eminent judges, was at one time a stenographer, and Charles Dickens, the great novelist, in his younger days learned something of it. The fact that Miss Whitton, who has undertaken this work and is a graduate of Queen's was at one time secretary to a minister in a government sitting opposite to the party now in power, and that she has not only attained a place and position in this country but certainly is recognized as one of the best known Canadian women social workers at Geneva, reflects no discredit upon her. During the last ten days she has been representing this country with great distinction in London. I mention that fact because I think upon reconsideration it will be found that if each one of us, when we have to give account for the work we have done, is able to say he has done his work as well, as faithfully and as fearlessly as she has, he will not have any cause to be ashamed of his record.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to say that I did not cast any reflection upon Miss Whitton because of the fact that she had been a stenographer. That was not my intention. I believe I complimented her upon being extremely capable, and it is no reflection upon anyone to accuse him or her of being a stenographer. I do think, however, that although she may be a first class stenographer or a first class graduate of Queen's, or an M.A-which I think she is-when she is taken out of that class and put into a medical department I say she is not competent. I do not think you can transfer a person from one profession to another. Neither am I speaking

unfavourably of the work that has been done by this organization. Under Doctor Helen MacMurchy splendid work was done; I believe I have said that. But now the work has been taken out of her hands and put into the hands of a university graduate. I believe my sentiments are reflected by some of the leading men in Toronto. I say that this work should have been placed in the hands of a medical man who would be more likely to have a better knowledge of the work than would a university graduate who had not studied medicine or was not even a graduate nurse.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I wish only to correct one statement. The work was not taken from Doctor MacMurchy. Doctor MacMurchy was retired because she had passed the age of seventy years; that is the reason. But in addition to that, the medical men are still doing the work they have always dome with respect to this service-possibly they are doing a little more. But the executive driving power behind it is that of the head of the organization selected and paid not by us- because we. pay her nothing-but by the voluntary contributions of an insurance company which regards the services rendered as being of the very first importance.

As I said before, I am not objecting to the grant, nor am I objecting to the selection of Miss Whitton. I think perhaps the society were particularly fortunate in choosing her, because she has been able to obtain an increased grant for the society from the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, no.

Well, what does the $3,000 mean, if it does not mean an increased grant? All of these are grants. I think she is to be commended for her ability to obtain an increase when others in similar positions are cut down. They all sustain the ten per cent cut, with the exception of this particular grant. I am not complaining, but rather commending her upon her ability to secure more money for the particular society in which she is interested, and I am assuming that she is doing splendid work. But I do wish to say to the Prime Minister and to the committee that the remaining grants are just as important as this one. In fact, the grant to the blind is in my opinion even more important, yet it has suffered a reduction, along with the others. That is my complaint at this time. Had this society of which for the moment Miss Whitton happens to be the representative received the same treatment I should not have had a word to say, except to express my regret that it was necessary to
cut the grants. I do think they are important, and I believe that sooner or later something will have to be done for the unfortunate blind in this country.
