An item went through the other day which I thought we should have had an explanation of, with respect to plant diseases. But here we are dealing not with a plant disease but with a pest disease, and the vote for it has been shot -well, I won't say where, but it is not all here.
I saw a dramatic photograph in one of the local papers of the battle that was going to be waged against insects this year. It was well done, one of the best displays of what this government should be doing but is not doing with regard to this pest that is right upon us. There are enough grasshopper eggs in Saskatchewan now to destroy two-thirds of our whole crop if they get a proper hatching, and they are hatching to beat the band at ninety in the shade. The battle is on and all the ammunition is absent so far as this government is concerned. All the government's artillery seems to have retired to bombproof caves.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is wholly incorrect.

We will see if it
is incorrect. Let us see if the Prime Minister

knows more than the Minister of Agriculture does about it. Let us see what they are doing in the United States to-day to combat this plague. Let me read to you what the battle is going to be like across the line. The government at Washington are on the ground; they are not two thousand miles from the battlefield with their ammunition reduced, as ours is in the form of these much reduced estimates now before us-less than half of what the vote was in 1931. What are they doing in Montana, Minnesota, Idaho, Nebraska and several other states? Here are the grasshopper plans of the United States as outlined at a meeting by Dr. J. R. Parker, of the Department of Agriculture of the United States, who discusses the control problem with the spring wheat millers. The item reads:
Dr. J. R. Parker, chief entomologist of the United States Department of Agriculture, who is in charge of all field work in connection with the government's grasshopper eradication campaign, met with a group of spring wheat millers in Minneapolis, March 6. to discuss the situation. He added that the house had passed the appropriation bill for the purchase of the necessary bran and other supplies but that the senate had still to act.
Here is another item headed "Grasshopper bait fund before senate committee." It reads:
Washington. D.C.-The $2,000,000 appropriation for grasshopper eradication, which is part of the general appropriation bill, was considered by the senate committee, March 5, with the probability of its approval. The bill passed the house last week. The Department of Entomology is prepared to contract for bran for making poison bait as soon as the authority is given, but can do nothing further until then.
I have not followed that up further to see what happened, but evidently the appropriation had passed one house and was likely to pass the other. That is their intention, at all events, across the line, but what are we doing here? If only our friends opposite had even pious hopes or intentions of doing something of this nature! But this government is leaving it to three impoverished provinces, which it knows are on the verge of bankruptcy, to fight the battle alone, except for advice and expert supervision. Hon. gentlemen opposite have retired into their cellar to let George do it, while in the United States the federal Department of Agriculture is out to fight this battle on the other side of the line to the tune of $2,000,000. Does the Prime Minister say I am not wholly correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes I do.

Supply-Entomology-Insect Pests

Then get up and
show me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am not quite sure
whether to be amused at or sorry for the statements that have just been made by the hon. gentleman. This is a vote dealing with pests. It has no reference to the hon. gentleman.

I will turn on the
juice so that I can hear this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is a vote for
" entomology, including investigations and inspections relating to destructive insects and pests." Technically there is nothing to be learned by Canadian scientists with respect to grasshoppers. Even the ordinary boy passing through school is able to tell you the habits of the grasshopper. All that was long since known. That the grasshopper is a pest is well known. That it has worked incalculable injury in the United States is also well known. It came to Canada from the United States. As a matter of fact large numbers that are now in the western provinces came to this country from the United States. The chief entomologist of the United States has been having a meeting with the millers and telling them that one house of congress has passed an appropriation and the other house is thinking about it. That is the illustration we are given of the high standard of excellence which characterizes the efforts of a government in some other country, entirely overlooking the fact that in the country in which the hon. gentleman lives steps were taken, not to meet the millers and have a talk with them, but to deal with the governments as to how the grasshoppers were to be destroyed.
What did they do?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They provided the money to enable that to be done. This government cannot go on to a man's farm in Saskatchewan nor can it legislate to do so. The provincial governments have sole and complete control in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. When they represent to us that loans are required and assistance should be given, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) takes the appropriate steps. I ask any hon. member from these provinces:	Has he any complaint to make as to what this government has done?

I will name one right
now. Last fall they came through my district and started propaganda on how to kill grasshoppers. They were asked by the municipalities if they would send in feed, but that feed arrived after the ground had been frozen and no work could be done. Two carloads of oats came into the municipality after the ground was frozen up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Which government was
that?
I suppose it was the provincial government, but you were supplying the money and they were not doing the work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) was a little premature. The thing to do is to get the provincial government started with a campaign of propaganda for the destruction of grasshoppers in the province. The program in Saskatchewan was somewhat more intensive than the one carried on in the United States, and what is more, it was carried on in the fall rather than waiting until the spring. If the hon. gentleman who knows so much about it will inquire as to what was done by the provincial government last fall and the steps taken to supply bran and poison and preparations for the destruction of the grasshoppers this spring, he will realize that at least it is not the fault of any government if the destruction is not complete. I have before me not only, the statement made by the minister as to the steps taken, but every request they have made to us for necessary assistance in order that they may discharge their duties, we have met. We have met those requests just as fully as the congress of the United States met theirs. Our scientists have been as active and the propaganda has been more intense than it was in the United States, and this was carried on last fall, not this spring.
There was a great deal of propaganda around last fall, but it was all propaganda.
Propaganda alone will not kill a grasshopper.

They went around and talked about what to do to kill grasshoppers, to do so much ploughing and so much work around the summer fallows in order to keep the grasshoppers out. Anyone who lives in that part of the country knows that after the middle of October you are quite likely to have a freeze-up and cannot do any work. The propaganda was started in September but the oats did not come out until the end of October or the first of November when the ground was frozen. Feed was not supplied to the people when it should have been supplied.

Supply-Entomology-Insect Pests

I should like to clear up this matter. Are we to understand that the assistance being given by the federal government for the destruction of the pest known as the grasshopper is not to come out of this item?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It depends upon what the hon. gentleman means. If he means the monetary assistance given to Saskatchewan, that was not under this item; it was under the relief measures.

I have in my hand the estimates for 1934-35, and these include a vote of S350,000 for entomology, including investigations and inspections relating to destructive insects and pests. In 1933-34 the vote was $399,946. I have the estimates for 1931-32-I keep them just for reference-and I find that entomology is not included with the administration of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act. In that year the vote for entomology is $35,000 and the vote for the administration of the act, S705.000. In 1930-31 there was a vote of $675,000 for the administration of the act and 830,000 for entomology. I could enumerate many others but I should like the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to tell the committee how it is possible, in view of what the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) has just said, to reduce this item to the figure it is this year.
It is just half what it was in 1931.
This year it is $350,000 as compared with $399,946 last year. What are the reasons for the reduction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There are always those who think that the expenditure of large sums of money indicates efficiency and effectiveness. The fact that $750,000 was spent one year presumably resulted in the elimination of the pests and the same amount was not required to be spent the next year. There should be a reduction in expenditure when the pest disappears. That is only logic. That is why the grant for the destruction of cattle affected with tuberculosis is much less this year than it was two years ago. That is why there will be an increase in the cost because of the outbreak in Quebec to which reference was made this afternoon. The same situation has developed with respect to insects and pests. This is all educational work; the federal government does not carry on the specific operations for destruction. It makes known and brings to the minds of the people knowledge, first, the character of the pest; second,

the habits of the pest; third, the methods by which the pest may be eliminated; and, fourth, educational addresses are delivered throughout the communities affected as to the threatened danger of a pest in their locality. All this has been done in this country for years, and the result is that a lesser sum is now being expended for that service. The sum asked for here is ample for the necessities of the service. It may well be that three years hence some new pest will rise up; there may be a Liberal government in power and it will be necessary to expend larger sums of money for its elimination.

You are confusing the
governments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I merely mention that in
passing. Knowledge is progressive, and the educational program carried on by the federal government is for the purpose of making known to the people the dangers incident to these ipests. The provinces have always had to deal with the specific destruction of the specific pest. In this instance the sum asked for is ample for the purposes sought to be achieved, but the actual destruction of the grasshoppers bears no relation to this vote. There has never been any complaint that there is lack of knowledge on the part of the people, and the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) has said that a great deal of propaganda was carried on last fall. I am able to express an opinion only from reading, and my knowledge is necessarily limited. But from what I know, from reading, as to what has been done in Saskatchewan and in some parts of Alberta and Manitoba, the propaganda was I thought very intense; and I ventured to think after they related to me what had been done, and after I had read what had been done, that they had made a particularly good job in anticipation of the spring. The danger time is in the spring of the year, and every possible effort has been made by the province to meet that situation. In fact, representatives of the government came here to request an extra loan in order to deal with the situation, and within the last few weeks an extra loan was made to enable the province to cope with its difficulties, because of its lack of financial resources to carry out what it conceives to be a very necessary and important task.
I do greatly deprecate the thought that the reduction in the size of an item indicates that there has been neglect, because we hope that as the years go by what we do with respect to herds of cattile in the country will obviate the necessity of the work being done over again.

Supply-Entomology-Insect Pests
I remember that only a few weeks ago an order in council was passed in which provision was made for retesting a small section of the country where a few short years ago a very large sum of money was expended to defray the damages that had arisen by reason of the herds in that locality having been infected with disease.
The whole problem is one of education, of appreciation of the difficulties, and of meeting the situation by adequate measures which scientists have devised and made known to the people. And this vote is ample for the purpose for which it is requested. It is not my duty to be familiar with every item in the estimates. The minister will be available if it is desired; he was called away, though he had intended to remain here. I would not for a moment ask this committee to adopt an item in respect of a matter of this kind in which they thought there had been dereliction of duty on the part of the government in providing ample funds to meet the necessities of the situation.

If the Prime Minister will look at the estimates he will find that he is linking together two items, tuberculosis and glanders. That is taken care of by the provision for health of animals. I do not wish to enter into any altercation with him, and I pay tribute to the staff of the experimental farms for the part they played last fall in doing the very thing which the Prime Minister says this vote is intended to accomplish, namely, spreading propaganda and educating the people. For the first time in twenty-eight years, in that part of the province in which I have been privileged to live, we have not had any such pest as necessitated anyone coming in.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Then no money had to be spent.

And that is what I am complaining of. In 1931-32 there was a vote of $705,000 and in 1934-35 the vote is only one-half of that; though the Prime Minister, I fancy, is as well aware as I am of the fact that so far as the west is concerned the grasshopper pest to-day extends from Eagle Hills, south of Battle river, clean south to the Saskatchewan river, or between the two Saskatchewan rivers. If he tells me that less money is needed to-day to provide the necessary education-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not what I said.

Then if it was necessary in 1931-32 to have $705,000 I should think that double that sum would be needed in
1934-35 for educational purposes.

I think I will have another little whack at this. I would not mind letting the matter stand until the minister comes back, but I would just as soon take a round with the Prime Minister now, especially since he has tried to discredit the statement I have made. I did not follow up the American vote, but I do know that when the Roosevelt government brings any measure in it is likely to go through, and a vote of this kind did go through last year. The states in the American union to which I have referred are like our provinces; they are right up against it financially, and when there is a plague like grasshoppers we find the American government coming to the assistance of the farmers to the tune of two million dollars. But this government retires, as I have already indicated, to its bombproof cave and reduces its ammunition by one-half for this class of work. We find that previously there were two sums, $707,000 plus $35,000, making over $740,000, and that is twice as much as we have for entomological purposes this year. If the Minister of Agriculture were here he would at least tell us that by a more efficient handling of the money they were able to do as much work as they did formerly with a larger vote. He has been trying to put that across and we have been accepting it, but not in toto, intimating that we did not quite accept it. But the Prime Minister has not had ingenuity enough to take that ground; instead he tries to discredit what has been done in the United States, where certain states are in the same position in this regard as our western provinces. The difference between the United States government and this government is that they came along with assistance to the tune of two million dollars whereas my hon. friends have retrenched to the extent of $350,000 for pests generally. That is the difference.
I will tell you what apparently the Prime Minister does not know. For the sake of argument we will say and it is actually so in normal times, that this work belongs to the states in the American union and to the provinces in Canada. But is there not a vast difference between voting $740,000 in 1931-32 when there were no grasshoppers and voting $350,000 when there is a grasshopper plague? The right hon. gentleman takes the ground that the reason the vote has been reduced is that the pests are receding; the less pests the less money needed. But are they receding? Does not all the evidence go to show that we are confronted with the worst invasion of grasshoppers in the history of Canada? My

Supply-Entomology-Insect Pests
right hon. friend says that they are receding. Well, that is what I call stretching a pretty long bow, though not, I hope, intentionally. But he merely says something for something's sake that doesn't amount to much. If it were the other way about, $350,000 voted when there were no grasshoppers in 1931-32 and $740,000 voted now that there are grasshoppers and other pests, that would be something that one would expect. But the right hon. gentleman is right up against it for an argument. When the Prime Minister of Canada cannot squeeze out of a hole it is because he is too far in to get out. With his facility of speech he can get out of almost anything, but he cannot wiggle himself out of the difficulty he has got into now. The fact is that the grasshoppers are there by the tens of millions, ready to eat the crops. The trouble was, the poison was not there last year for the last lap. Talk about propaganda 1 How much propaganda will it take to kill a grasshopper? Far more than my hon. friends can spread. If you don't get the dope into the grasshopper how are you going to get rid of it? What was lacking in the fight last year was poison and a good deal of the effect of the early campaign was lost because the grasshoppers were allowed to reach the stage where they took flight, going into and beyond the region of my hon. friend from South Battle-ford. The more you kill when they are small the less there are in the flight season. The flight was carried to within ten miles of my own farm, and I am sure that if the grasshopper campaign had been strong enough last year their flight would not have extended half the distance it did. But in the absence of sufficient poison the grasshoppers grew and took flight, seeking pastures new. And they found them in that and other western regions. Moreover, they laid their eggs wherever they lit, and the laying was good. Yet we are preparing to fight them by reducing the estimate for entomological pests instead of giving a special vote as they did in the United States. That would have been a great battle in the time of the war if we had prepared for it by reducing our ammunition, our large ordnance, our staffs of men and our money vote, but that is the way we are preparing to fight Ihe grasshoppers. No wonder they are thriving! They are real grasshoppers, hopping all over our prairies and developing into locusts, we are told, while our friends are sitting in this chamber reducing the estimates and claiming they are doing their full duty. If our provinces were in good shape I would not make any complaint about this, but they 
are in a very bad state; they cannot for lack of money do as well as they know how to do. Where is the peace, order and good government relief vote that it cannot be drawn upon? Can we not keep order among the grasshoppers as well as elsewhere? Why can we not draw on that provision in this emergency?
It has just flashed upon me that this is the way in which my hon. friends are going to reduce the wheat acreage and production- let the grasshoppers have their fling. It will be an act of God, I suppose, instead of an act of the Bennett government, that is the situation. The grasshoppers are on the prairies in such a superabundance that unless some absolute miracle happens we shall not begin to fill our quota; we shall be able easily to give possibly 50,000,000 to the Argentine unless something is done to help the provinces fight the grasshoppers when they hatch, and they are hatching now. If my hon. friends think I have not produced a case against this government, then we shall have to take a gimlet, perform a surgical operation on their craniums and pour the information into them some other way. The tell tale estimate is there; no one can challenge the figures I have given. If conditions were normal the United States government would also not be helping their states, but conditions are not normal there and they are not normal in Canada. That shows the difference between the government at Washington and ours. I have a right to protest. I am glad the Prime Minister has given me the opportunity to explain the matter while he is present, because I would not care to talk to the Minister of Agriculture in the way I have done to my right hon. friend. He is the head of the government, very much so, and I hold him more responsible than the Minister of Agriculture for the disgraceful way in which the agriculture estimates have been reduced in the last four years. I hear an hon. member opposite groaning. Well, he ought to groan. What occupation other than agriculture have we to rely upon to bring back to normal the economic welfare of this country? What estimates have been reduced more ruthlessly than those of agriculture? I do not know. Talk about economy! This is a penny wise and pound foolish policy, reducing the estimates of the one branch of our country's activites on which we rely the most, that represents one-half of the people of Canada and feeds them all in addition to what we export. Yet my hon. friends are chewing and screwing those estimates down and then pretending that they are not doing so. That is what makes me angry. They get up in broad daylight, or rather in gaslight-and it is gas

Supply-Entomology-Insect Pests
that they gave us-telling us they were doing their full duty when the facts and figures deny that right to the hilt. The Prime Minister tried to discredit my statement because I gave the facts in regard to the United States up to the date stated, asking where I got the information and indicating that I did mot know whether the legislation went through. I know it went through last year and there is not one chance in ten thousand that it did not go through this year. Now, if the Prime Minister wants to retire and hand things over to the Minister of Agriculture, he is at liberty to do so or to give them to anyone else he likes.

The hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) is not the only one who has had to fight grasshoppers; we had them in Nova Scotia forty years ago. My hon. friend opposite, the member for An-tigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) will I know recall that. They were there so numerous they stopped the railway trains day after day, and that was not confined to one year. We did not then go yelling to the federal government for help; we looked after and met the situation ourselves. My hon. friend opposite has apparently reached the age and stage where the grasshopper is a burden. Why not go out and fight them as we did? He whines and demands assistance for everything that happens and blames the government for its happening. Let him get to work on the grasshopper problem and stop his growling.
That must be one of the Rocky mountain locusts we have just heard from.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In this evening's paper the following appears on the front page:
Are Critical Days For Western Crops
The next two weeks will be the most critical ones affecting crop prospects in western Canada. The dry weather with high winds has caused *considerable top soil drifting.
Wheat seeding is practically completed and that of coarse grains well advanced. Grasshoppers are beginning to hatch in some districts, but elimination measures are well in hand. The northern empire of the Peace River reports conditions and prospects are excellent according to the weekly crop report of the Department of Agriculture, Canadian National Railways.
From what is the prime minister reading?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
From the front page of this evening's paper. "But elimination measures are well in hand." I have received no complaints in regard to elimination measures. While I am always ready and willing to assume responsibility for any acts of 74726-203
the government or of myself in an official capacity, I think most intelligent people who have listened to the discussion for the last five minutes will wonder just what this country is coming to. I ask this chamber: What do thoughtful people in the gallery listening to this think? I console myself with the proverb "Answer not a fool according to his folly." Age has its claims to respect and in this instance to silence. If the United States spent 82,000,000 federally to destroy grasshoppers, this vote of 8350,000 multiplied by twelve would make 84,200,000. and if you divide $2,000,000 by twelve, the United States having twelve times the population of Canada, we would be spending less than $200,000, but we are actually spending $350,000.
It is not all over the United States; it is only in certain states.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is not all over Canada either, and it is over a wide area in the United States. If the United States spent on the same basis as the Canadian figures suggest, they would be spending more than $4,000,000 federally. This $350,000 is for the whole of Canada. The mistake is to assume that it is limited to a particular area. Might it not be the fair thing in dealing with a matter of this kind to ask whether any demand or request made by those affected had been refused, whether any suggestion as to assistance had been declined, whether there had been an entire disregard of an obligation that legally belongs to others but that morally, by reason of financial conditions, is accepted by the federal government? I wonder sometimes whether after the last five minutes it is realized and recognized the amount of money the dominion government has put into Saskatchewan in the last three years; I wonder if it is realized the extent to which we have been subject to adverse criticism both public and private; I wonder if it is realized the way in which we have met the situation, because we have had faith in the future of that great agricultural province whose population is some 900,000. We have cared directly at one time for as many as 300,000 men, women and children, providing them with food and clothing through the long winter days and weeks and months, and the reward given for the efforts made, not by the government but by the Canadian people, is to be traduced, abused and slandered because they have thus done. It is their money, largely from eastern Canada, supplied through the purchase of bonds, that has enabled this to be done. Is it any wonder that at times we find it increasingly difficult when in endeavouring to deal with a situ-



Supply-Entomology-Insect Pests
ation of this kind we are confronted with statements such as those to which we have listened to-night? Let us at least be fair. Here is a calamity that has come to a part of Canada which Sir William Butler spoke of as the great lone desert, the part of Saskatchewan south of the Saskatchewan river. We have had drought; we had the binder of the soil destroyed by cultivation; that great alluvial deposit was dried and ground to an almost impalpable powder that the winds picked up and threw high in the air so that the trains passing through were covered with dust. Yet the courage of the people has been sustained and maintained. Ten millions, fifteen millions, reaching into the twenties, loaned, assuming direct obligations, caring for the people-all these things have been done, and there has been no complaint of which I have knowledge that the assistance rendered by this dominion to Saskatchewan in respect of grasshoppers has been inadequate. In the face of that I put it to my fellow Canadians whether they think that exhibition and that attack is calculated to encourage those upon whose good will and good feeling towards western Canada we must rely in our time of peril. I leave that to the committee.
I say with respect to the vote for entomology that it meets every demand. I am not confusing the two votes; I used the other by way of illustration. I am perfectly well aware that the variation in the amounts of votes depends on the extent to which work is undertaken. The work which was undertaken and paid for through the relief measures in Saskatchewan during the fall results not in complaint but, in reports in the newspapers that elimination measures are well in hand. Against that we have these denunciations of individuals, of myself, of the Minister of Agriculture, alleging failure of duty, failure to understand and appreciate the situation. That is helpful! That is constructive! That is calculated to encourage those who have risked their money for the purpose of trying to assist us-and by "us" I mean those of us who live in western Canada, that being my home as well. If at times one gets discouraged after listening to the tirade I have listened to to-night, in view of the knowledge of what we have done and are still endeavouring to do with respect to that drought stricken area, who can blame us? I leave that in the hands of the committee.
When the Prime Minister gets into his last ditch he always starts up the sob sister stuff. That is what he is doing now.
Carried.

Not until I am through. My right hon. friend is trying to make out that Canada was doing more than the United States. How much of this goes to buy poison? That is what the west was short of last year and is likely to be again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not one dollar of it.

Everything is done except the one thing necessary. They can feed them with propaganda, but they will fatten on that alone, if you don't get the dope into them. The right hon. gentleman's remarks were aimed in my direction. Slander. There is no slander. Every word I have uttered is doubly true, and proven by the records and official estimates-
Question.

-and by the statements of the hon. members for South Battle-ford (Mr. Vallance) and Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly). The vote is now not half, less than half of what it was in 1931, and they try to make out that they are doing more. The Prime Minister has tried to figure it out so that it will look better by taking the forty-eight states of the American union and trying to make it appear that we in Canada have been giving more than they are giving over there. But the forty-eight states have not all got grasshoppers, any more than the nine-provinces of Canada have. It is just a lot of bunk that cannot be supported by anything but a whine. Think of the horses being allowed to die in the country, crops being put in with mules and cows and steers and oxen and anything that can go into a yoke or collar, and yet the elevators full of grain within a gunshot of these dead animals! Hundreds and thousands of them dying, and the elevators filled to the top with wheat that cannot be sold and that they don't know what to do with. But the animals know what they would do with it if they could get a gallon a day to keep them going through the winter, even if it is wheat. Letting them die! Supplying seed grain to put in another crop and then sitting back knowing that there is not one chance in ten thousand that the grasshoppers will not eat it all up again, and not supplying one dollar's worth of poison to help. Then my right hon. friend starts that whining that he can pretty nearly put across, as he has done two or three times this session, but he cannot to-night because the record is against him. He ought to be totally ashamed of himself. I say again what I said before, that neither

Supply-Entomology-Insect Pests
the national government in Washington nor that in Ottawa would have needed to help either the states there or the provinces here if the conditions were normal, if the provincial revenues were half as buoyant as they used to be. What is needed is to provide lots of poison and lots of help to distribute it. If the right hon. gentleman cannot see it, that is only evidence that this government is about the greatest aggregation of-what shall I call them?-something that can produce a marketing bill some of which no one can understand, not even themselves.

I have heard the Prime Minister on more than one occasion eulogize the people of western Canada, and I was rather disappointed to hear him to-night reminding this house of what eastern Canada has done for the west. I would like to tell him something from a different point of view. I see him smiling, but he smiles from the chair of a law office in the city of Calgary, most of the time. I want to take him back to the great open spaces where people are living 150 miles from a railroad. I want to tell him of the contribution that these people made to the making not only of western Canada but of eastern Canada. I am pleased to be able to say that in the twenty-eight years I have been there I have made my contribution, and I resent the Prime Minister's telling me and the people I represent what eastern Canada has done for them. I would like him to visualize the God-given wilderness we went into twenty-eight or thirty years ago, 100 or 150 miles from railroads, and without facilities, many of us with only an ox cart. We have built highways; we have built railroads, churches, schools, towns, villages and hamlets. We have created billions of dollars' worth of wealth, and where has it gone? Those people he talks of are sitting in those lone homesteads to-night with very little equity, if any, in what they have created, and the Prime Minister tells us what eastern Canada has done for the west. He should go out and tell them that. Where has this wealth gone? Can he tell me where it has gone? I should like him to tell the people in the west where it has gone. After all their work and privation we have to sit here tonight and they have to sit in their homes and listen to what eastern Canada has done for them. Put western Canada in the position, as I have heard him say before, where they have purchasing power, and in eastern Canada our industries will hum. Make it possible for the 300,000 farmers west of the great lakes to have 12,000 or S3,000 purchasing power, and what will happen? I am not

blaming this government, but I am blaming the Prime Minister for the statement he has been trying to get across as to what eastern Canada has done for the west.
I would like to tell him about my own province. What do the other eight provinces get from the province of Saskatchewan? We have to take our coal from Alberta.

One million tons were

Yes, from the Estevan
field going into Manitoba. We take practically all our lumber and fruit from British Columbia. We take nine out of every ten carloads of groceries from Manitoba. We take implements of production from Ontario, and some from Quebec and the maritime provinces. Yet out of the whole production of the province of Saskatchewan Canada does not take twenty per cent, and for the remaining eighty per cent we must find a world market. Then the Prime Minister wants to tell us what eastern Canada has done for us. .No, Mr. Chairman, I resent it. I have listened to him in this house pay one of the greatest tributes I ever heard anyone pay to the pioneers of western Canada, but when I listened to him remind them to-night of what eastern Canada has done you cannot wonder that I rise in indignation.

I do not speak very often in this house, but I think it is time some hon. members opposite should stop and realize that in Canada there are some provinces besides the western provinces. There are people in Ontario who need money just as much as the western people need it, so far as that is concerned. Only a couple of years ago we gave them a five cent help on their wheat, but never got any thanks for it. They talk about grasshoppers, and to listen to the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) one would think that there were grasshoppers only out in the west. My friend in the east told the committee that his constituency had been bothered with grasshoppers, and we have some in Ontario. But when the grasshoppers strike Ontario we look after them, and we do not complain. I believe the origin of a good deal of the trouble out in the _ west can be traced to the west. So far as this discussion is concerned, I do not think there should be any line drawn between the-east and the west. I have a good deal of respect for western members, and particularly those sitting on this side of the house. L

It seems to me that the people in Ontario and the other eastern provinces are getting very little thanks for what they are trying to do for the people in the west. I have all kinds of faith in the west, and I do say that the remarks by the hon. member for Melville were unbecoming to him; they were very much out of place. I do not intend to take up any more time, but' if I got hotter I could say more about it.

We are a long "way from bugs, Mr. Chairman. I suggest you use your authority to stop this discussion, which will not help us any, and is merely setting the east against the west. We are getting nowhere. I appeal to my hon. friends to allow the discussion to drop. Such recriminations will not promote good will between the east and the west.
I have listened with a good deal of indignation to what the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Yallance) has had to say. He asked what the east had done for western Canada.
I did not ask that; the Prime Minister told us.
Well, I rather think you did, and I will tell you. In the first place, we bought it and paid for it. In the next place we built three railways to it.

The four original provinces.

a return of the natural resources of your western country. There is no end to what you fellows think you ought to get. You exhibit very little gratitude-

It is very strange, Mr. Chairman. I sent a letter to the minister about the matter on March 13 last, and I have received no answer as yet. The letter gave full particulars of the case. I have a copy of the letter here which I will read. I was wondering why I did not get any reply. I thought it was 'because the minister was investigating the matter. The letter is dated Ottawa, March 13, 1034, and reads:
Dear Mr. Matthews:-	_
You will no doubt remember my asking you on the floor of the house regarding the matter of whether a vessel entering Canada from another country has to pay customs dues on the valuation of the ship and engine in the event of the vessel being registered in the United' States and coming to Canada to be used for profit here.	_
The matter I have in mind is in connection with a fishing boat named Klekane whose owners operated part time in Canada and part time in the United States, moving back and forth according to the fishing.
It is owned by two brothers; one lives in the States and the other lives in Vancouver.
It is registered in the State of Washington as a United States vessel and operates in Canadian waters as a Canadian one. and I was informed that on account of the fact that it paid customs duties away back in 1919, I believe, it has a right thereafter to go and come as a Canadian vessel. Surely this is not correct. The vessel cannot be registered in both countries at the same time. In my opinion, at least, if a vessel is registered in Canada it remains so until it registers in another country and having done bo loses Canadian registry and takes on the registry of the other country.
A great many protests have been sent to me regarding this matter and I understand that this is not the only vessel that is allowed to go and come in this manner.

I would be pleased if you would have this looked into and a ruling given, and may say in closing that I am of the strong opinion that no vessel can be registered in two countries at one and' the same time.
I have no recollection of receiving that letter. It may have come to the department, of course, but I do not recollect having seen it. I shall certainly see that my hon. friend gets a reply.

The hon. member for
New Westminster (Mr. Reid) asked concerning overtime, referring particularly to the payment of overtime to full time officers while temporary men were allowed to go. There is no doubt the temporary men were what are known as seasonal officers who are taken on at a number of frontier points during the season of heavy highway traffic. Both regular and seasonal men have to be on duty Sundays and holidays, and when they cannot be compensated by being given time off they are paid the regular overtime rate of seventy-five cents per hour less the ten per cent deduction. It would not be possible to eliminate entirely the payment of overtime as there are a number of places where the additional services required' do not warrant additions to the staff; therefore it is more economical to pay overtime. There has been a considerable reduction in the expenditure under this head during the past year or so, and I can assure hon. gentlemen that every effort is being made to reduce expenditures still further.

I asked this question because
of complaints which were made to me last year and I think the year before that seasonal men had been cut down while more overtime had been paid to those regularly employed. It did seem rather hard that those who were engaged the whole year should be taken out to these boundary points and thus deprive the seasonal men of work. I should like the minister to look into this with the idea of permitting these seasonal men to earn a little more money.
